As far as I have been able to discover, we have only six mills in operation in that entire area. I would like to know how it comes that these 79 timber berths are held without any operations being carried on. I do not know whether they have a right to hold them without doing any work upon them or not. They should not have. But there are six mills being operated and a lot of the timber which they are producing is being sold south of the American line. While lumber is being exported from our own province, a great many people, are demanding that an embargo be put upon British Columbia lumber so that they cannot export it. If the Government would hand over the timber limits in Saskatchewan to the Government of that province and let them deal with them the provincial government could, if they saw fit, make such regulations as would give to our own people the use of their own lumber, and in that way a great deal of the discontent would be allayed.
The situation is this. As long as these timber berths are controlled by the Dominion Government there is no development. The provincial government has not the right or the power to adopt a policy for the development of those resources. I saw a question on the Order Paper, which was answered by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) about what statement was made by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) prior to the election. There is no question about it, he promised that these natural resources would be handed
over to the people of the province. I myself heard him make that statement. In view of the uncertain conditions which that promise has created, a promise which has not yet been fulfilled and which would involve an entire change in the regulations covering the control of the timber areas, can we expect that the men who own these timber berths, and wealthy men generally, are going to invest their money in the development of these resources? Most undoubtedly not, because if there is one thing more than another that money is scared of it is indefiniteness and uncertainty. The Government, in the interest of the people of Saskatchewan, should end that period of indefiniteness and uncertainty as quickly as possible and hand over to our province these timber resources so that other regulations may be formed to encourage the proper development of these areas and thus give to our people what really belongs to them.
Now there is far more timber than that. I happen to have here testimony on the point from Constable Eaman of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, who has been all through that country and who states:
Below Lac La Ronge is a great area of splendid timber.
Then again he states:
In 1916 the value of the out was $1,226,000. Many of the areas of timber are not yet within reach of a market. For example, there is an area of 13,000 acres at Montreal lake estimated to contain 120,000,000 feet that cannot be reached until communications are established.
All this timber is there, but for the lack of a few miles of railway our people are compelled to suffer and our progress is retarded in the way it is. So much, Mr. Speaker, for that.
We have more than timber in that section of the country, we have a great deal of coal. True it is not the very best, as yet, but i't is being developed. The Government have very wisely, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Fort William, embarked upon the policy of demonstrating the feasibility of briquetting the lignites~~Of southern Saskatchewan. A great many complaints have been made by our people that the work is being carried on very slowly but I am not one of those who join in that complaint. It is a demonstration plant and nothing else; and I want to say that I would sooner take a little longer time and have 'the demonstration made a complete success than hastily launch into something and find that it results in failure. I am glad to know that the Government are

taking their time with this demonstration plant and carrying out the experiments properly. So long as they are making substantial progress I will be very content, and I only hope that they will continue the work and get through with it as soon as they possibly can. I am satisfied that as soon as the- demonstration plant, which will manufacture some thirty thousand briquettes in one year, has been established and proven to be a success, we will htve dozens of these plants established all over southern Saskatchewan and southern Manitoba. But lignite coal is not the only coal we have in southern Saskatchewan;-and I am sorry the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) is not in his place to-day because I would like to- have drawn his attention to one peculiarity which he, probably more .than anybody else, ought to deal with as promptly as he possibly can. To-day we are bringing all our bituminous coal from Alberta and our anthracite coal from the United States. In the city of Regina we are about six hundred miles from the bituminous coal mines in Alberta, and the city of Winnipeg is about three hundred and sixty-six miles farther away still. It so happens, however, that within the last two years a new coal field has been discovered within two hundred miles of the city of Regina, and within two hundred and fifty miles of Winnipeg. That field is now known to contain at least twenty million tons, and some estimates run as high as Sixty million tons. That coal is better coal than any bituminous coal ever yet mined in Alberta. I have a copy of the analysis that was made by the Government and I have seen samples of the coal. It differs in this one respect from the other coal-that while the lignite coal at Estevan is covered with .some twenty-five to fifty feet of earth this particular deposit is covered with some two hundred feet. As hon. members can very easily see the increased weight of earth covering it has resulted in greater pressure -.nd thereby given a better quality of coal. In addition to that this particular deposit is perhaps of greater age.
, Now what are the conditions? As soon as the farmers in the locality discovered this coal they incorporated themselves into a company and fixed their capital at half a million dollars. They have already spent some $80,000 in .sinking shafts and are prepared to go on with operations, but unfortunately they are about eight miles from a railway and the Canadian National railway at that. Last year the Canadian National did undertake to build a spur 
from Lampman to Peebles which would go directly through this area, and 'they graded some eight or ten miles of the line from the south. About twelve miles of railway have still to be built before we get the Canadian National railway down there, but as far as I can see there is no intention of building it this summer.
Complaint is being made that we cannot get men to do this work, that there is no labour available. In this connection I will read an extract from a letter received by me from the secretary of the- recently organized mining company who, as I have already said, have spent somp $80,000 in development work:
I received your letter to-day and was pleased to get news regarding the railway. I note what you say regarding the labour situation. I have been deluged with requests to obtain work for men and teams on this line. We have been in the dry belt for the last three years and the farmers are only too anxious to get out and make some money with their teams. We can supply ail teams and the men to grade this road if the Canadian National railway will lay the ties and steel and oversee the work. Don't let them bluff you on the labour situation on this line.
Now this coal field is within two hundred miles of the city of Regina, and we want to buy that fuel but cannot get it. The city of Winnipeg also would be only too glad if these mines were developed, but it can be readily understood that with the mines eight miles from a railway it is utterably impossible for the company in question to develop them. Yet the mines are right at our doors and we have no means of doing what we want to do. If these mines in Saskatchewan were under the control of the Provincial Government I am quite satisfied that that Government, would quickly take the necessary action to place this coal within the reach of the people who want to buy it. Of course, I quite understand that the railway companies do not want these mines opened. They would prefer to collect rates on freight coming six hundred, seven hundred or eight hundred miles away rather than .-on freight coming a distance of only two or three hundred miles. The former is quite an inducement for' them; and that is one of the things we have had to contend with in days gone by to a far greater extent than some of you people in the East have any idea of. I urge the Government to adopt a policy calculated to bring this coal within our reach just as soon as they possibly can.

What is the quality of the coal that the hon. gentleman has

been speaking of? Has he an analysis of it?

The thickness of the seam is seventeen feet but I have not the analysis before me. When this debate is over, however, I will procure and submit the analysis to the hon. gentleman. It demonstrates that this is not bituminous coal such as Alberta possesses.
I do not want the information personally, I want the country to get it.

I can easily obtain it for the hon. gentleman. My view is this: There is room for the development in Western Canada of every coal mine we have got. The progress of the country has been, and will be, such that it will take everything that every coal mine there can produce to keep up with the demand for coal. If we can make our people generally satisfied and put them into a prosperous condition every mine in the province will have all that it can do.
But it is not merely coal mines that we want to see developed in our country. We want a development policy also with respect to our farm products. So much has been heard about No. 1 Hard wheat that some people think the province of Saskatchewan cannot raise anything but that cereal. There was a time probably when we did not do much more than raise No. 1 Hard wheat, but we are very quickly getting away from that type of farming. I am glad to see it because personally I am one who does not believe in putting all our eggs into one basket. A short time ago I asked the Board of Trade of Regina to give me a statement showing what they thought could be done in the way of industrial development in Western Canada. Now all Boards of Trade are generally pretty sensible bodies of men and when you come to the Board of Trade of Regina you have got something pretty good. ' The Board of Trade has declared:
Another very important industry in the development of this country are cold storage and packing plants. Saskatchewan has at the present time 352,989 cows, 926,342 other cattle, 134,177 sheep. 521,240 swine and 8,000,000 chickens. The total value of livestock, including poultry, of all descriptions, is $271,377,044, and not an abattoir or packing plant of any size in the country. It is true there is a small packing plant at Moose Jaw, one at Prince Albert and one in Regina, but these are totally inadequate to take care of the needs of that industry in the province.
In the year 1917. as compared with 1916, Saskatchewan more than doubled the number 65
of cattle marketed. Of cattle, hogs and sheep Saskatchewan marketed 303,254 head, as compared with Manitoba's 229,292 and Alberta's 144,734. Manitoba's increase for the year over 1916 was 33,825, Alberta's increase was 52,361; combined increase for the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta, 85,186. Saskatchewan's increase alone was 93,545, thus, notwithstanding the splendid increase made by Manitoba and Alberta, Saskatchewan did better than either or both combined.
And not an abattoir or packing plant of any size in the whole province! I wish those words could reach a few of our wealthier men, to show them what a splendid opportunity presents itself there for the investment of some of their money. I feel satisfied they would make just as big profits out of plants established in Regina as they do out of many of the plants which they have here.
What about Calgary?

I do not care whethei they establish plants in Regina or anywhere else so long as they get them in Western Canada. I want to see the whole of Western Canada prosperous by the development of our natural resources. I am sure that Calgary Will not object to see Regina prosperous, and I know we are very glad to see Calgary going ahead. I believe Calgary by reason of its splendid situation and its natural advantages-water powers all around, timber within easy distance, and situated on the edge of the greatest market on the continent-I say I believe that Calgary is destined to be one of the largest industrial cities on the North American continent. Provided, of course, that the people of Calgary get busy and take advantage of the opportunities confronting them. If instead of developing those opportunities they sit around idle and apathetic, of course they will not get anywhere.
I have stated why I am supporting the resolution offered by the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). We have unlimited natural opportunities in the West. Our clays are unquestionably the best in the world for manufacturing pottery of all kinds. If any hon. member doubts my statement, let him read the records of the Department of Agriculture. I remember, a little more than two years ago at a meeting of the city Commissioners of Regina, a bright young man came before us. He told us that he had been for the past three years representing the Dominion Government in investigating the clay deposits of the province of Saskatchewan, and he said: I thought I would come in -and tell you that, in my opinion, you have the best clays that


can be found anywhere for the manufacture of pottery. I wish to draw the attention of the Government and of the investing public to the fact so that those natural resources may be developed.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to cite the opinion of a geologist in reference to our asphaltum, and,I would like it to sink into the- minds of hon. inembers. My authority is Dr. Bosworth, a British geologist, who is now chief geologist for the Imperial Oil Company. He published a brief account of his findings in Northern Alberta in the "Petroleum World" of February 1916, in which occurs the following paragraph:
" The exposure of asphaltum visible along this river is greater than all the other known asphaltic outcrops, pitch lakes and oil seepages in the world put together."
Yet we are doing absolutely nothing with those resources ! That is what I object to. Seemingly we have no policy at all so far as our natural resources are concerned. I ' urge upon the Government to take this matter up as quickly as they can in order that they may adopt a policy for the development of these great natural resources, or if the Government do not feel justified in developing them directly, I would suggest that they take measures to bring before the investing public the fact that these opportunities are awaiting men of capital and enterprise and will ensure them magnificent returns.

Mr. Speaker, I presume I will not be out of order in prefacing the few remarks I have to offer by approaching the subject from the viewpoints of people holding diverse political creeds. I think we can now unhesitatingly come to the conclusion that we have passed the time when individualism was the groundwork of all political policy, and when it was dogmatically said that laissez faire was the only policy for Governments. The last four years of the war unquestionably demonstrated what governments are able to do in some respects. It may be urged that governments in developing natural resources are verging on Socialism, which is the other extreme. It seems to me that such a contention would not be well founded, because the socialistic doctrine as we now have it from one end of the world to the other is based on the form of government at present in control in Russia, and although the advocates of Socialism call it by different names, they all agree on the fundamentals of the Soviet government.

But between those two extremes there is a legitimate field for governmental endeavour. We have seen in the last few years how such countries as Germany and the United States went ahead industrially a great deal faster than Great Britain. In this connection, I may say that I have no qualms of conscience in benefiting from such lessons as Germany before the "war was able to give us. While references to the war are perhaps becoming somewhat obsolete,
I know our soldiers never hesitated to take from the German soldiers any new fighting wrinkles they might have, whilst giving the enemy some of their own. I believe that if to-day we adopt some such middle course as government supervision or assistance in developing our natural resources, we will be taking a sound course and one which will greatly rbdound to the advantage of Canada.
Through accident, or it may be through policy, as one may care to view it, we have to-day control of a very extensive railway system and are rapidly completing the building of a magnificent merchant marine. Having got thus far, we must develop our natural resources and our exportable products if we are to make our railway and our fleet pay their way.
We have to-day a further incentive to action in that we have a national debt of over two billion dollars, and it seems to me in no way can we liquidate that indebtedness with greater certainty than by adopting the sound policy of developing our natural resources. I need only point out the example of Ontario, where the stumpage charges are bringing an enormous revenue into the provincial treasury.
With a policy of developrnent, if the work is done under private ownership, the question of definite royalties and payments of that sort arises, and these should bring in substantial revenues to the State. There is no other country in which the natural resources are greater than those of Canada in proportion to population, and therefore I have no difficulty in coming to the conclusion that we stand on firm ground when we say that it is a good general policy for the Government to develop its natural resources, to give assistance possibly to private persons who go into that business, and in any event to have a strong policy, a policy which should bring this country to the financial condition to which it is entitled much earlier than would be reached under ordinary conditions. It is true that we have a policy at present; that we have done something. We have the Advisory

Council for Scientific and Industrial research, -which is doing good work so far as it goes. We have the Department of Mines which is doing excellent work, the Geological Survey Branch, the Commission of Conservation and other similiar institutions; but we have never given these bodies sufficient power or scope to enable them to carry on their work properly. I believe I am correct in stating that if any private business corporation owned the resources of this country, they would not have this more or less haphazard and immature policy of development which now pertains in Canada; a private enterprise with these vast resources at their disposal would go at them in a scientific and businesslike way, because we must all realize to-day that one thing which the war has brought forward is this, that the chemists and chemistry in business have come to the front as they never have before. Therefore, the Government would be well advised in bringing forward a definite, firm and comprehensive policy. There may be those who will say that at present, when the war is just over, we should not spend large sums of money on this sort of work; but I do not think that is sound economics, because only by spending large sums can you bring about greater development and get a revenue larger than any sum you might spend. To be penny wise and pound foolish is not good policy.
Then there comes the question which has already been discussed by other speakers, that of handing over our resources to the provinces. I will say, without hesitation, that this is something which should be done. It is something which has been promised, and that promise should be implemented, but I am concerned not so much with that aspect of the question as with the fact that something should be done now. Let some decision be reached whereby either the Dominion Government or the provincial governments will realize their responsibilities and will be able to bring down now a policy for the years that are to *come. The point in regard to that question is that something definite should be done now; but as nothing has been done, the responsibility to-day is the responsibility of the Dominion Government, and to that Government we, therefore, address any remarks which we may have to make. If the Dominion Government should, in the near future, hand over to the western provinces their natural resources, there still remains for the Dominion Government a great field in the way of industrial research, of standardization, of exporting the results of
these developments, and to all these problems the Dominion Government could very well give considerable attention.
It is natural, in speaking of this subject, that I should refer mainly to Alberta from which I come. It is true that up to date our basic industry has been agriculture; and while I may not have all the facts in connection with this subject at my disposal, it appears to me that the Government must have a policy for exporting our wheat from that part of the country next year. I do not know where that wheat will be sold, except such portions of our high grade wheat as are required in the United States to mix with their wheat, unless it be sold on the continent of Europe, and I do not know of any country there which is able to finance its purchases, except by accepting the very great difference in exchange which now exists and which, as a rule, you will find them unwilling to accept. The Government must realize not only that they will have to handle this situation next year, but that they must take care of the export, of that equally important feature of agriculture, namely, the cattle industry. I can see no fundamental difference between the agricultural industry and the live-stock industry; we can never develop Western Canada as a wheat-growing country alone and at the same time expect that our soil will last for years to come; we must have both the cattle and the wheat. We cannot consume all the cattle which we already raise and the surplus must be exported in some way or another. Whether we shall have to revert to barter and exchange or accept long term notes of foreign governments, we must, if we wish to keep our wheat - and cattle business on the basis on which we now have it and at which the extent of our land and the fertility of our soil demand that we carry it, face that difficulty now.
There is also in Southern Alberta the question of irrigation. A large tract of .land is there mapped out ready for irrigation, and while I am not prepared at this moment to say what is the duty of the Dominion Government, or the duty of the provincial government in connection with that matter, the Dominion Government should at all times be ready to co-operate with the provincial government in bringing along that much needed development.
What I wish to speak of more especially to-day is the mineral potentialities and possibilities of Alberta. One, perhaps, gets the impression that Alberta and the other Western Provinces are entirely agricultural provinces, but that is far from the truth.

Last year Alberta was the third province in the Dominion of Canada as regards its mineral output, and in 1918, the output of minerals in Alberta amounted to $23,000,000.
It is true that we have had no exhaustive survey of our iron ores in that province, but iron ore indications are in evidence right from the Crow's Nest Pass up through Calgary to the far North where on the lakes large quantities of iron are to be found. It is very possible that we shall find that iron to be of a low grade, and it is for this Government to deal with the question whether low grade iron can be scientifically reduced as a commerical venture. I hope I shall not weary the House if I read just a very few lines from the report of the Honorary Advisory Committee on Scientific and Industrial research in regard to this question. The report states:
The investigation of the reduction of iron ores by gases, under the supervision of Professor Stansfield, of McGill University, has advanced to a stage which promises important results bearing on the utilization of ores of low grades so abundant in Canada. There is but a small supply of high grade iron ore in the Dominion, which is emphasized by the fact that 96 per cent of all the iron ore smelted in Canada is imported, this importation including, of course, that obtained from Belle Isle, Newfoundland. The total quantity of high grade iron ore on the Globe available is, through its use for producing iron and steel, diminishing at a rate which makes its exhaustion a not far distant event, and in consequence it will eventually be necessary to turn to those of lower grades for the supply of ore for the industry. If the smelting could be effected on an industrial scale at a reduction in the cost which would offset the disadvantages at present attendant on the utilization of these lower grade ores it would make available, immediately or in the very near future, the immense quantities of such ores in Canada. The Research Council regards the solution of this problem as of very great importance to Canadian industry and as justifying a protracted experimental investigation carried on on a large scale.
The reason why I have read this is that I think the Government should make a most thorough survey of the possibilities of iron ore in Alberta. They should not hesitate in aiding scientific men in endeavouring to reduce those low grade ores as a commerical venture, because if that can be done, we have in Alberta coal which is practically illimitable in quantity and easy to mine, but which is now valueless because -we have no use to which to put it. Possibly when these investigations proceed further, it will be found that Alberta will be an excellent place in which to put those investigations into operation first, because with coal which is practically valueless and

in such abundant quantities that you can go into practically any area of the province and erect your plant, sink your shaft and get your fuel, it is possible that low grade ores can be handled economically as an industrial proposition. The House has heard many times how much coal we have in Alberta. We have in that province onte-eighth of all the coal in the world. It is not all lignite; it is anthracite, bituminous and lignite in practically unlimited quantities. Those who are perhaps not familiar with our lignite coal think that it is in the nature of a new experimental substance which one can use for heat, but it is real coal after all.
It is an excellent coal for domestic use, just as good as, and in my opinion better than, any kind of anthracite or bituminous coal. In 1918 our production of coal amounted to 6,000.000 tons, the highest of any province in Canada.
Two things are required in order to increase the development of our coal in the province of Alberta. One is to extend the market area, and the other is to encourage coal using industries in that province. With regard to the extension of our market area, that brings us to the question of our railways. I am not one of those who would be continuously clamouring for reduced rates in order to please the people of this country, but I do say this: When rates can be reduced and the result from such reduction shall be the development of natural resources which will increase the commodities which the railways will haul, I think we are talking pretty sound economics when we ask that such reductions be made. 'It is true that the railways, requiring traffic westward, desire to bring anthracite coal to Western Canada from Port William and have wheat as a return haul from the West. It is against that influence that it will be necesary for us to fight. The Drumheller association of coal operators have made a most reasonable request to the Railway Commission lately to this effect:	That "during the months of
April, May, June, July and August, when no wheat is moving, and when cars and equipment are standing idle throughout Western Canada awaiting the time when they will be used for hauling the crop, some reduction be made in the coal rate from Alberta down to Port Arthur. That would serve three purposes. First, it would utilize the railway equipment; secondly, it would enable the mines to run the year round, and thirdly, it would obviate the difficulty which occurs every winter when the whole of West-

ern Canada tries to be supplied at the one time with coal from the mines, and often without success. It has been proven that our coal will stand up for six months, and it seems to me a reasonable and proper policy for the Railway 'Commission or the Government to reduce the rate during this period in order to get these three excellent results. Our vision perhaps soars to the day when we will supply the country further east than Fort William. If the carbonizing and briquetting experiments which are now being conducted on Saskatchewan coal are successful, they will unquestionably be successful with Alberta coal, and with those experiments a success our coal in the form of briquettes, equal in heating value and every other respect to anthracite would surely come east of Fort William and go a long way towards bridging the great central part of Canada which in 1918 imported no less than $71,000,000 worth of coal from the United States.
In connection with the briquetting process we have the by-products of distillation. We get tar, on which is built up the analine dye industry. In view of the quantity of coal we have in Alberta, if we can get that coal produced, briquetted, and sold, we will have an enormous quantity of this tar base on which to build up our analine dye industry. Ammonia sulphate is also derived in large quantities during this process of distillation, and at the rate we are tilling the soil in the West it will be only a few years before we shall need this excellent fertilizer in that country.
In Alberta we have the Alberta Industrial Congress. It is an association for the purpose of attracting industry to Western Canada. Some may think that we are a little early, but it must be remembered that we have already on the plains of Western Canada about two and a half millions of people, which is a rather good market for young industries to start on. We have coal which is practically theirs for the asking. We have every expectation that our population will not only increase, but multiply itself in the next twenty-five years. I think it should be part of the Government policy to attract attention towards the industrial possibilities of Western Canada. It is true that the Government have voted a sum towards that congress for this year. While on this point, I think we could well afford to have one on the Pacific coast, a Pacific trade commission similar to the trade commission operating on the Eastern coast. I know from personal experience what a great trade could be worked up with the Orient, and I
would direct the attention of the Government to those possibilities.
We have cement, water powers, lumber and pulpwood in great quantities throughout that country, but as other hon. members have spoken of these resources I shajl say nothing further about them.
Our clay products in Alberta are of the very greatest importance. In 1918 Canada imported $6,700,000 of clay products, and Alberta produced in that year $381,000 worth. I am certain there is a great future for the development of pottery, bricks, and clay products in that province.
Then we come to the question of oil. The pursuit of oil is very similar to the pursuit of gold. It is one thing which seems to stimulate the imagination and energies of mankind more than anything else, and many incidents are bound to happen in the development of an oil field. I believe it often takes from twenty to twenty-five years of prospectirfg and drilling before an oil field is established. In Alberta we produced in 1918 over $100,000 worth of oil, all of which has been sold. We can say that the indications from one end of the province to the other, starting from the asphaltum sands, and going almost down to the fields of Montana, show that we have enormous oil resources in that country. The Government then can come to the conclusion that they have an oil field in Alberta. What should they do to develop it? Should they endeavour to explore and drill and develop it themselves, and then turn it over to good advantage to private companies? Perhaps that would not be an unwise policy. It is a matter for the consideration of the Government. The Government have already provided that leases shall only be granted on payment of a royalty to the Government. I think the Government made a mistake in not placing a maximum on that royalty. As it is, it is to be fixed by the Governor in Council from time to time as it may determine. You go to a firm and ask them to start work in that country, and they will say to you: Until the amount of royalty is fixed we do not know where we are at. There is no easier way of losing money than by sinking it into holes from which you get nothing. Those who spend large sums of money are entitled to know what, royalty the Government intends to take. I want it to be understood, however, that I am thoroughly in accord with the policy of taking a royalty.

There is another matter in regard to oil. Alberta does not participate in the bounty of one and a half cents per gallon which the more favoured oil of Ontario gets. Our oil is of such a superior quality, it is of such low specific gravity, that it does not come within the qualifications set forth in the Order in Council governing the bounty. Though it is true that our oil is worth three times as much per gallon as the oil of Ontario, we are not asking that we be given three times as much bounty, but simply that our oil be not discriminated against, and that in that area which is not yet developed, and where men are needed to go on with the enterprise, no discrimination be made against us.
Natural gas exists in Alberta in unlimited quantities. This is not so important immediately, because it can only be used as the population increases and a donrestic market is built up. I might point out that it has lately beep discovered that from the Calgary gas field alone a quantity of helium valued at $3,000,000 could be extracted annually. At the present moment this new gas is going- up the chimney. The cost of a plant to save this product will, I understand, not exceed $200,000, and the use to which this gas can be put is becoming increasingly wide.
At this point I want to make this statement: Eastern Canada asks us from time to time to buy its produce, probably at a little higher price than the produce of the United States, in order that we may develop Canadian industries, and that the workmen of Eastern Canada may be assured of a livelihood. We may be willing to do this, but at least we ask that if people from the East request these things of us they shall in return assist us in marketing our commodities and extending our coal market, and in increasing the production of the natural resources of our western country. This strikes me as a most fair proposition, and one that is well worthy of consideration by the Government. It is also one that might well be carried out to allay, .to some extent, the present feeling that they are being unfairly dealt with, which exists in Western Canada.
In conclusion, let me express the opinion that there are some definite things that could be done. A request was made that a Natural Resources Bureau should be created, a Bureau of Scientific Investigation and Scientific Standards,, similar to that which exists in the United States and largely similar to that in England. It ap-

pekrs to me that the evidence taken last year before the special committee is undoubtedly sufficient to convince us that our industrial development would be greatly benefited by the institution of such a bureau. Some permanent policy of development should be undertaken by the Government and, if necessary, some responsible minister of the Crown should be in charge. I think that we should have a "national consciousness" driving towards the development of our resources, and that our policy should be complete. It should not be haphazard but comprehensive. With that stimulus and inspiration from the Government, private enterprise would feel a great deal safer; and with a sound policy behind it, capital would be disposed to go in for the development of the country's natural resources. Our geological surveys of the various ores and minerals of the country should be more thorough. Our investigations into the briquetting of lignite and the reduction of low-grade irbn ores should be exhaustive, and we should not be parsimonious in our expenditures in providing help to our scientists engaged in this work. I believe that if the Government would realize the industrial potentialities of Western Canada and bring down a sound and strong policy, our natural resources would be developed and you would have in Alberta not a one-sided community, not a community with one line of industry alone, but a well-balanced community which would have within itself all those varied lines of endeavour which exist in Eastern Canada. Under such circumstances, you would have a community that would think in the same terms as do the people of Eastern Canada. The day is not far distant when we shall have twenty or twenty-five million people in Western Canada. Immigrants are coming from all parts of the world. We want to be, above all else, Canadians, and the development of the natural resources of Western Canada will put an end foreveT, I think, to the annexationist and the secessionist, whether he carries on his propaganda under the political or under the economic guise.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. H. KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Permit me to say a few words in support of this motion. I should like, instead of speaking, on the matter generally, to confine myself to one particular resource, and that is iron, which is one of the most important basic elements of industry. Let me lay down a few facts. In the first place, we have in Canada an

enormous supply of low-grade iron ore; secondly, we have no high-grade iron ore. The last mine we found was the Helen Mine, and the high-grade ore there has been exhausted. Thirdly, of the total .amount of iron ore that is used in this country, viz., over two million tons only four per cent is mined here. We might ask ourselves the question, why is it that with millions of tons of iron ore only four per cent is mined in Canada, notwithstanding that private capital and governmental enterprise have endeavoured to get it into the market? The answer is rather simple; it is because our ore is low-grade, and we must do something to raise its metallic content; in other words, we must get it into commercial use. Otherwise, that ore will lie undeveloped until high-grade ores in other parts of the world are exhausted, and in the meanwhile Canada will have to depend upon outside countries for its ores.
The question is, is that advisable? Is it worth while for us to consider the advisability of mining our own iron ore and trying to get the ninety-six per cent taken out in our own country? What are the benefits derivable from the mining of iron ore? First of all, the wages are spent in the country. Probably for every ton of ore mined, three or four dollars is spent in wages and supplies, and to-day that is all going out of this country. Of course, it goes without saying that this state of things is not advisable if it can be remedied. The railway, earnings on that iron ore are also going out of the country. How much better it would be if these iron deposits which are knowm to exist all along the Canadian National Railway system were developed and used, and the Canadian National deficits to that extent turned into productiveness. It is well known that the iron ore raihvays are the most profitable railways everywhere. Between the passenger receipts and additional freight receipts, the coke and lime- _ stone, etc., that enter into smelting, a reasonable amount is always to be estimated as profit where there is an iron ore railway operating. To-day we annually provide for deficits for the railway, and surely it would be better to make these railways earn money by developing the iron in the country.
Another benefit that would be derived from such development would be the increase in population. You cannot mine one or two million tons oi ore without having a large number of people engaged in connection with the work, and if we develop the industry that lies at our hand it is reasonable to assume that we could increase the population probably by fifteen or twenty thousand people, who would represent a certain national value to the treasury of Canada. Each person is known to be of some value to the state in the customs duties he pays, and the revenue which the state derives from him. It would pay to subsidize iron ore production in Canada. If we did we would also get a national benefit through increased railway revenues and the general prosperity of the country, and furthermore wTe would at once remove our present complete dependence on the United States. All of our iron ore in Ontario now practically comes from the United States. We are far from the Maritime Provinces. They get their ore from Newfoundland. Ontario must get hers from the United States. The time is not very far off when they may put -an embargo upon iron ore as they have done upon coal, and for two or three years we will be helpless until we develop our low grade iron ore. It seems to me that we cannot be very far wrong in urging the development of our ores now.
Another benefit that would accrue from it would be that which we would derive in connection with the question of exchange. We are paying for this iron ore to come into the country from the United States. We are also paying something like $150,000,000 per annum for steel and iron products from the United States. If as a result of a little inducement, additional to what there is now, to develop our low grade ores, and perhaps thereby find some high grade ores, we get into this country three or four more iron mills operating, increasing the general prosperity in that business and producing that much in our own country, we are benefiting the country and we are not sending out all that money to buy these products.
There is another point that should not be lost sight of. There is a difference between mining iron and mining coal, in that every ton of coal that is mined and used is lost to the country at large except only that which has been used in making something else. But when a ton of iron ore is dug out of the ground and put into circulation the country is that much richer. It does not disappear. It is something which goes on from one form to another continuously until it oxidizes away, which takes a long while. The country is richer for every ton of iron ore that is dug out of the ground and which iremains on top of the ground.

We are paying subsidies to almost everything-to railways, cables, zinc, lead, and oil. We are talking about subsidies to flax. We pay subsidies to agriculture in that we maintain experimental farms and spend $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 a year upon them, and rightly so. Surely we could spend a million or two in subsidizing the production of iron ore in this country. If we gave a dollar a ton by way of subsidy for every ton of iron ore that was produced and smelted in Canada we would get it back and we would simply be doing for that industry what we are doing for many others.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House further than to say that I believe that that this is a time when Canada should map out a forward policy in regard to its natural resources and particularly in regard to its low grade iron. We know we have low grade iron. We have not been able to find the high grade iron, but we have hundreds of millions of tons of low grade. The sooner we develop a forward policy (even to the extent of subsidizing), getting that iron upon the market, getting our own people working upon it in our own country and spending what we have here instead of outside, the better it will be for our country. I do sincerely trust that the Government will at this session give this matter its most careful consideration and that it will realize that for every dollar that we spend in benefiting the iron ore industry it will get more than a dollar paid back into its own treasury.

Mr. Speaker, the hour of adjournment is near at hand, but I do not want the discussion to close without making some observations on a question which I consider as important as any that we have discussed in the House this session. Any member of the House who may have had doubts about the natural resources of this country should have had them removed as a result of the enlightening addresses which have been made by the members who have preceded me. I am going to confine my remarks to the coal resources of this country. I had intended making a few observations on some other of the resources that exist in the province of Alberta but I do not think I will have time to do so this afternoon. We have been reading in the press lately-and I presume the people who live in the province of Ontario have been reading it with a great deal of fear-about the probable cost of coal in this province next year. The coal supply of Ontario is in the state of Pennsylvania, and there is no doubt that that sup-
[Mr. Keefer. 1
ply is being gradually and perhaps rapidly, depleted. Ontario and Quebec must look for a new source of supply for coal. I do not know whether the House is familiar with the fact that in the province of Alberta, which is generally known as a wheat growing and stock raising province, we have 87 per cent of the coal resources of the Dominion of Canada, and that it is estimated that that province has within the same area the largest coal resources of any place in the- world. I am not advancing that as a promoter of mining schemes; I am simply quoting the facts that are given to us by the authorities in the Department of Mines of the Federal Government.
When we s; eak of Ontario and its need of fuel we naturally think of Albeita and its great resources. The Government here, and the provincial governments, will have to do something to bring western coal into Eastern Canada. I admit at once that the present price of western coal transported from Alberta into Ontario, would be so high as to prevent the people of Ontario from considering its general use for fuel purposes, but I believe it is possible to overcome some of the obstacles that do exist in this regard. I believe that Ontario and Quebec can stave off the possibility of the depletion of their supply from Pennsylvania if they co-operate in encouraging the use in Western Canada entirely of Western Canadian coal. At the present time we know that in Manitoba, Pennsylvania coal is used to a very great extent. If that supply was cut off from Manitoba the western mines could have a market which would help them, while at the same time, it would relieve the consumers in the Eastern Provinces. I have been advised that even the Dominion Government, in asking for tenders for coal for some of their buildings in Manitoba, stipulate that it must be Pennsylvania coal; so that they are not encouraging the use of western Canadian coal.
What does it mean to Western Canada - to have the market of the three Western Provinces?-I am not speaking of British Columbia because British Columbia has its own coal. We have been accustomed in this Parliament to hear of of the industrial troubles in the mines of Alberta practically every year.
One of the reasons for our industrial troubles is the lack of a permanent market. As the situation stands at the present time, coal is mined in Alberta almost wholly during the early fall and winter months. When we come to the spring and summer months the mines are closed and the min-

ers have to go out and look for work in other occupations. Under circumstances of that kind you cannot expect to have settled conditions in the industrial world in so far as it concerns the miners. I believe that even with coal mining developed to the extent to which it has been in Alberta-and I may say that under existing conditions there is no doubt that the coal mines have been developed to double the capacity of the market that is offered their output-if the governments, the railways, and the' commercial organizations were to get together and try to reach an arrangement whereby the coal produced in Western Canada could be utilized to the greatest possible extent throughout the Western Provinces, the result feould not but be beneficial to the country at large. Because if we had the market in Manitoba which at present is supplied by Pennsylvania coal it would help o maintain the coal mines on the prairies in operation duiing the greater part of the year.
Another matter I would like to emphasize in this connection is, the question of transportation. At present our coal is being mined and shipped at about the same time that our grain is being shipped, consequently the railroads are -not dn a position to Ihgndle coal satisfactorily and cheaply. If we were able to have summer mining of coal in Alberta, the railroads should be in a position to haul the coal much more cheaply than they do at the present time, because it would be >a slack season in transportation eastward. All that is necessary in that regard is to educate the consumer and the dealer in Winnipeg and 'in other western cities to store- coal in the summer for use in the winter.
Might I also mention the fact, which has been advanced by people who have investigated the coal industry in Alberta, that if it was possible to operate the mines month in and month out during the year, whereby thg miners would have steady occupation and a regular income, it would be possible to produce coal a good deal cheaper than it is produced at the present time.
The points I have urged should be kept in mind: there should be encouragement of the use of Western Canada coal dn the West in order to help the eastern provinces in obtaining their supply from Pennsylvania; a solution of the transportation problem should be provided by the operation of the mines in the summer months thus guaranteeing steady employment to , the miners; and a campaign of education should be conducted to establish to the 66
people in the extreme parts of Western Canada that the coal produced on the prairies, or at least a great -amount of it, compares very favourably with the coal produced in the state of Pennsylvania. I know that from experience because I have lived in Ontario and used Pennsylvania coal. I have been using Pennsylvania coal in this city during the past winter, and I certainly do not consider that the coal mined in the southern part of the province of Alberta takes any secondary place to the coal produced in Pennsylvania. But we must educate the people to the need of using our western coal.
Another point I would like to bring out is this; it would be important, in order to educate the people and get them to use Western Canada coal, to grade the coal because as it is at present all Western Canada coals go on the market and they are ''considered to be prairie coal and are bought as though they were all alike, and of course that is not the case. Certain of oiir Western Canada coals are of much higher quality than others and if there was a grading of coal it would be very helpful in educating people to their use.
I presume the Acting Prime Minister is desirous of making some observations on the resolution that we have been discussing this afternoon, and therefore I do not want to unduly extend my remarks although I had intended speaking at much greater length on the question of our resources.

Move the adjournment of the debate.
Mr. BELA'ND: That would kill the debate, we should never reach it again. "
It has been suggested that I should move the adjournment of the debate.
The hon. gentleman can speak until six o'clock if he wishes.

We are asking this Government to encourage the development _of coal and all the natural resources that we possess in this country. I might point out the fact that to-day individuals as well as companies are investing probably all their means in the development of our natural resources throughout Western Canada. Men are going up into the mountains and looking for ore. They are going about the prairies searching for oil. They 'are investing their money in digging wells in the effort to obtain oil, and. in rnanj* instances they are exhausting their entire



financial resources for that purpose. I think therefore it is only right that we should ask not only the Federal Government, but the Provincial Governments where they are in control of the natural resources, to encourage in every possible way the development of our natural resources.
What is the need of Canada at the present time? We have a great, debt in this country. How are we going to meet it? We are told to produce. We can produce in the factories, on the land, and in the mines of this country. We have great natural resources that only need to be developed in order to enrich this country; and if we could only develop those resources to the extent of one-fourth of their value at the present time we would have no trouble in meeting our obligations as a nation. There is no cause for any person in this country to be discouraged about the future of Canada. All we need to do is to move around this Dominion to realize the great resources we possess; and we cannot help but become prouder of our country and cannot help but glory in the fact that in Canada we have as great wealth and as great opportunities as are to be found in any land in the world to-day. What is requisite is to encourage the development of those resources, and give an opportunity to the people to take advantage of the wealth that is in the country, and there will be no need for the Government to worry about the future of Canada and no need for the honest, capable and ambitious citizen of Canada to worry' about it either.
Now that six o'clock has been reached; may I ask, what will become of this debate?
